headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 4 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.46–0.99), suggesting that Vitamin E is associated with a lower risk of renal cell carcinoma. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 75.25%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

studies.Reference: No association between fruit, vegetables, antioxidant nutrients and risk of renal cell carcinoma.
studies.Authors: Bertoia M, Albanes D, Mayne ST, Männistö S, Virtamo J, Wright ME
studies.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile of total vitamin E intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: completed a 276-item dietary questionnaire that included questions on frequency of consumption and portion size

sample_size.excerpt: At baseline, 27,062 male Finnish smokers aged 50-69 years completed a 276-item dietary questionnaire that included questions on frequency of consumption and portion size. During up to 19 years of follow-up, 255 men developed RCC.

cases.excerpt: During up to 19 years of follow-up, 255 men developed RCC.

effect_size.excerpt: Despite a large range in intake, no association was observed between fruit, vegetables or antioxidant nutrients and RCC risk. For example, multivariate RRs and 95% CIs for the highest versus the lowest quartile of intake were 0.79 (0.55-1.14), 1.23 (0.85-1.79), 1.09 (0.74-1.60), 0.83 (0.57-1.21), 1.09 (0.73-1.64) and 0.99 (0.67-1.46) for fruit, vegetables, total carotenoids, total flavonoids, total vitamin E and vitamin C, respectively (all p values for trend > 0.05).

sample_size.excerpt: In the current analysis, we included all participants in the clinical trials and the observational study except for women who enrolled in the Dietary Modification clinical trial (n = 48,835) who had a history of any cancer other than nonmelanoma skin cancers at study entry 7 , 10 , 12 or who had implausible energy intakes (<600 or >5000 kcal daily) at baseline (n = 4067). This resulted in an inclusive total of 96,196 women in our analytic cohort.

cases.excerpt: In total, 240 women in the study population were diagnosed with RCC during follow-up. The median follow-up for the entire sample was 4339 days (approximately 12 years), and the median time to kidney cancer diagnosis was 2518 days (approximately 7 years).

cases.excerpt: Sociodemographic and baseline health characteristics and nutrient intake levels of 1142 cases and 1154 controls in the eligible study population are presented by race in Table 1 . studies.Title: Effects of supplemental alpha-tocopherol and beta-carotene on urinary tract cancer: incidence and mortality in a controlled trial (Finland).
studies.Reference: Effects of supplemental alpha-tocopherol and beta-carotene on urinary tract cancer: incidence and mortality in a controlled trial (Finland).
studies.Population: male smokers aged 50-69 years from southwestern Finland

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: A total of 29,133 male smokers aged 50-69 years from southwestern Finland were randomly assigned to receive alpha-tocopherol (50 mg), beta-carotene (20 mg), both agents, or a placebo daily for 5-8 years (median 6.1 years). Incident urothelial cancers (bladder, ureter, and renal pelvis; n = 169) and renal cell cancers (n = 102) were identified through the nationwide cancer registry.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: Incident urothelial cancers (bladder, ureter, and renal pelvis; n = 169) and renal cell cancers (n = 102) were identified through the nationwide cancer registry.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Neither alpha-tocopherol nor beta-carotene affected the incidence of urothelial cancer, relative risk 1.1 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.8-1.5) and 1.0 (95% CI 0.7-1.3), respectively, or the incidence of renal cell cancer, relative risk 1.1 (95% CI 0.7-1.6) and 0.8 (95% CI 0.6-1.3), respectively.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: Neither alpha-tocopherol nor beta-carotene affected the incidence of urothelial cancer, relative risk 1.1 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.8-1.5) and 1.0 (95% CI 0.7-1.3), respectively, or the incidence of renal cell cancer, relative risk 1.1 (95% CI 0.7-1.6) and 0.8 (95% CI 0.6-1.3), respectively.
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: randomly assigned to receive alpha-tocopherol (50 mg), beta-carotene (20 mg), both agents, or a placebo daily
extraction_supporting_text.design: We studied the effect of alpha-tocopherol (a form of vitamin E) and beta-carotene supplementation on urinary tract cancer in the Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene Cancer Prevention (ATBC) Study
extraction_supporting_text.continent: male smokers aged 50-69 years from southwestern Finland
